items.content:
[This article was first published on Bioconductor community blog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

In the report on our Japanese workshops, I explained why our Crowdin integration had become difficult to maintain. Keeping executable R Markdown lessons in sync required file conversions, translation synchronisation and reconstruction of buildable lessons. I remain grateful for Crowdin’s support. We are now moving to PLaMo-based AI translation directly in the lesson repositories, with code and markup protected and community review on GitHub.

I am introducing a new AI-assisted translation workflow in the bioconductor-translations organisation, built around PLaMo 3 Translate and review on GitHub. The first lesson is Introduction to data analysis with R and Bioconductor, with published editions in Japanese, Spanish, Simplified Chinese, French and Urdu. These editions are open for community review and improvement.

What is PLaMo 3 Translate?

PLaMo 3 Translate is a family of large language models developed by Preferred Networks (PFN) specifically for translation. PFN’s November 5, 2026 technical article, PLaMo 3 Translate: World-Class Translation with Open Weights—Here’s How We Built It, explains the development process and the release of downloadable model weights.

PFN trains the models on source–translation pairs and further refines them to prefer better translations. Smaller models also learn from the 31B model through distillation. The family supports 53 languages and can take surrounding context and a glossary into account. These features fit our lesson workflow: we can supply nearby explanations and preferred technical terminology when translating a passage.

The models come in four sizes: 0.8B, 2B, 8B and 31B parameters. Our workflow uses pfnet/plamo-3-translate-8b-MLX-4bit, the 8B model in a 4-bit MLX format that reduces memory use for local generation on Apple silicon Macs. The model weights are distributed under the PLaMo Community License.

Explore the five language editions

The introductory lesson covers organising data in spreadsheets, using R and RStudio, manipulating data with dplyr, and visualising data. Each language edition has a lesson website for learners and a repository for contributors:

Language Read the lesson Contribute on GitHub
Japanese Japanese lesson bioc-intro-plamo3translate-ja
Spanish Spanish lesson bioc-intro-plamo3translate-es
Simplified Chinese Simplified Chinese lesson bioc-intro-plamo3translate-zh-hans
French French lesson bioc-intro-plamo3translate-fr
Urdu Urdu lesson bioc-intro-plamo3translate-ur

Our Crowdin project also received Portuguese translation contributions, and I am grateful to everyone who contributed them. I am sorry that Portuguese is not included among these editions: the PLaMo translation model we currently use does not support Portuguese, which is absent from its supported-language list.

Translation coverage and review are still in progress. Some setup pages and interface labels remain in English. At the time of writing, the published Urdu episodes are available, but that repository’s updater configuration and translation guide still refer to Japanese and need adaptation before being used to regenerate Urdu text.

How the translation system works

  1. Read an English source revision. The translator reads the upstream lesson’s R Markdown files from a Git revision without checking it out over the translated working files.
  2. Reuse matching translations. Each translation repository stores its versioned translation memory in translation/seed-cache.json. This JSON file stores previous translations and review statuses by source passage and episode. Matching records can be reused, while new or changed prose is sent to the model.
  3. Guide terminology and protect structure. A language-specific glossary and contextual guidance help disambiguate terms. Code blocks, inline code, link destinations and lesson markup are protected during translation, and structural checks run before lesson files are replaced.
  4. Review and build. Maintainers inspect the translated text and memory changes, build the lesson, and commit the reviewed result. The translator itself does not commit or push changes.

Shared terminology in glossary.json

Each repository keeps its preferred terminology in translation/glossary.json. For example, the Japanese repository’s translation/glossary.json contains source and target term pairs, mapping “data frame” to “データフレーム” and keeping “Bioconductor” unchanged. The translator passes these pairs to the model to guide terminology consistently across episodes. Contributors can propose glossary changes through pull requests. A glossary change requires fresh generation for machine records on the next update; matching reviewed records retain their wording, so terminology corrections must also be applied to the reviewed translation memory where needed.

Update a translation yourself

To update a translation yourself, follow translation/README.md in the repository for your language. These documents cover environment setup, fetching the English source, previewing changes, generating translations, reviewing the results and building the lesson:

  • Japanese: translation/README.md
  • Spanish: translation/README.md
  • Simplified Chinese: translation/README.md
  • French: translation/README.md

For Urdu, the updater configuration and documentation caveat above still applies.

For example, in the Japanese repository, after configuring the upstream remote as described in its guide, a maintainer can run:

git fetch upstream main
uv run --locked scripts/translate.py --source-ref upstream/main --dry-run
uv run --locked scripts/translate.py --source-ref upstream/main --update-memory
git diff -- episodes translation
Rscript scripts/build.R

The dry run shows which passages can be reused and which need translation, without generating new text or writing lesson files. The --update-memory option saves new translation records to translation/seed-cache.json and source provenance to translation/source-manifest.json for review. The local runtime cache under .cache/translation/ is ignored by Git. Other editions may use a different remote name, so follow translation/README.md in the repository you are updating.

The translator also checks for local edits and stops before overwriting an edited lesson. Small build adaptations are recorded separately with checks against the expected source. Images, datasets and episode ordering still need separate maintenance when the English lesson changes.

Local generation, reusable community knowledge

The workflow pins the model revision and locks its Python dependencies, recording the source revision and model provenance with the translation resources.

Generating new translations with the current implementation requires an Apple silicon Mac, Python 3.12 and uv; the first model download is about 6 GB. Planning updates and replaying cached translations can run with Python 3.12 alone on other platforms. Reading lessons and contributing a review on GitHub require no model installation.

The translation memory gives community review a lasting role. You can inspect the records in the Japanese translation repository’s translation/seed-cache.json. Newly generated records are marked machine. After checking a record in translation/seed-cache.json, a reviewer can mark it reviewed so that its wording is retained for matching source text in the same episode and language pair, even when model or glossary settings change. The French translation repository’s translation/README.md explains this review process.

Help make the lessons better

A successful build shows that the lesson can be rendered, but readers and instructors still need to check its meaning. A translation can sound fluent while changing an exercise condition, using an unfamiliar technical term, or losing an important distinction. The Simplified Chinese translation repository’s translation/README.md explicitly identifies its initial translation memory as machine generated and needing review.

If you use one of these languages, please try an episode and compare it with the English lesson. We especially welcome help with:

  • Language and terminology: suggest clearer explanations and vocabulary familiar to your local research community.
  • Exercises and teaching: check that questions, solutions and instructor notes preserve the original learning goals.
  • Corrections that carry forward: help maintainers update the glossary, context guidance and translation memory alongside the lesson text.

Open an issue in the relevant repository with the episode name, the passage you are referring to, and a suggested correction or explanation. Pull requests are welcome too; please follow that repository’s contribution and translation guides. If you are interested in reviewing translations, adding support for another language, or translating another lesson, join the discussion in the #documentation-translation channel on the Bioconductor community chat.

Thank you to the original lesson authors and maintainers, and to everyone translating, reviewing and teaching these materials. This work builds on the community’s translation efforts described in the Japanese workshop report and is supported by the Bioconductor Developer Champions Program.

items.content:
[This article was first published on Data Analytics and AI Archives - Giles, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

TLDR: Weighted by population, the rule of law has slipped globally since 1996. India and the United States contributed a large part to this decline, while China’s net impact was negligible thanks to a recovery from the mid 00’s. Countries with a stronger rule of law tend to be wealthier, and those where it improved were more likely to grow faster, but there are plenty of exceptions to the rule, with China experiencing higher growth than might be expected from changes in its rule of law score, alongside Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Guyana and Myanmar.

How AI was used: AI was used to write the first draft of analysis included in this post. I then collaborated with AI to refine the post until it resembled what I had in mind: the majority of writing is therefore my own. AI also was used to put the post in a format compatible with WordPress.

Background

One of the reasons consulting suits me is that it provides me with an almost unlimited number of rabbit holes to get lost in. One such example that came up in 2025, was a project exploring the links between economic growth and the rule of law for the Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law and the Law Society of England and Wales. If you’re interested in exploring this further, I’d recommend Dr Lopez-Gomez’s literature review, which was a key outcome of the project.

This is the fourth post in my series on the rule of law (see earlier posts: 1, 2 and 3), with previous posts intended to demonstrate themes that this and future posts rely on, including that:

  • The Worldwide Governance Indicator’s (WGI) Rule of Law index provides a reliable proxy for the World Justice Project’s (WJP) measure (with greater coverage over a longer period); and
  • It’s probably not a good idea to solely use pairwise relationships for exploring how the rule of law interacts with other outcomes as these things are hard to measure, co-determined and probably operate within an interdependent system of institutions.

Four themes

Although I had grander plans when I first started drafting this post, I’ve scaled back my ambition to focus on four themes that provide useful context for future posts:

  • Globally, the rule of law has deteriorated since the mid 90s.
  • Countries with stronger rule of law are wealthier.
  • Countries that improve their rule of law tend to grow faster.
  • But, the rule of law isn’t a necessary or sufficient condition for economic growth.

Here be dragons

To avoid the need for weasel words and vague descriptors it’s worth remembering that cross-country analysis is a minefield:

  • Institutions like the rule of law (etc) are hard to define and measure: Institutions are the rules, norms and conventions that shape, constrain and guide human behaviour and interactions. Institutions can run from the grand rules and expectations that ensure peaceful democratic transitions after an election to the mundane social norm that ensures Bill from Accounting doesn’t microwave his tuna salad at lunch. Whether the former is more important than the latter is a matter of taste, but being all encompassing, interdependent and hard to define also makes institutions difficult to measure. This is particularly true for perception-based measures as someone asked how well the rule of law works is likely to be thinking about democracy, accountability and government effectiveness too, while potentially making qualitative judgements that lean towards accepted Western models of governance.
  • Interesting things tend to be correlated with one another: As institutions like the rule of law operate within an interdependent system (see last post), everything tends to be correlated with one another whether or not they are causally related. Economic growth probably depends on the quality of a country’s legal system, but the legal system itself likely also depends on economic growth too as it influences the resourcing available for government to invest in it. This makes it difficult to talk about the rule of law as a discrete characteristic independent of other institutions.
  • National statistics obscure the relationships that matter: Cross-country statistics are not always representative of specific actors or the underlying causal mechanisms that we’re interested in. For instance, economic and social relationships sometimes transcend the nation-state (the unit of focus for cross-country analysis).
  • Institutions are sticky and slow moving: We consider a time series of data running from 1996 to 2023, which is just short of three decades. Although this might feel long-run enough, leading studies in the field cover much longer periods e.g. 100+ years (see 1 and 2). In practical terms, this might mean that the strength and direction of relationships examined here might not generalise over longer periods.

But, I haven’t picked the themes covered here by accident: each of them tells a story supported by the literature, which I’ve done my best to cite throughout.

Project setup

Data

The rule of law measure is the Rule of Law dimension of the World Bank’s WGI, 2025 release, which covers 1996 to 2024.1 The WGI’s RoL attempts to measure the quality of contract enforcement, property rights, the police, the courts and the likelihood of crime and violence. The WGI’s measure has been selected on the basis of it covering a larger number of countries over a longer period. Earlier posts in the series also indicated it provides a reliable proxy for the WJP’s more comprehensive RoL measure. The data can be downloaded here.

Statistical measures, namely GDP per capita (PPP), GDP per capita growth, population and oil and gas rents, along with each country’s World Bank region, have been drawn from the World Development Indicators via the wbstats package. They were downloaded once, on 22 October 2026, and saved, so the results don’t change when the World Bank revises its figures. A snapshot of the data used here can be downloaded here.

Country income classifications were the earliest classifications available from the World Bank’s historical classification data (available here).

Pacific island small states are the World Bank’s group of that name, taken from its current country classification file (CLASS.xlsx, downloaded on 7 November 2026 from the same page).

Access to the sea, as the share of each country’s population living within 100 km of a coast or a navigable river, and the malaria index came from the geography dataset of Gallup, Sachs and Mellinger,2 downloaded on 7 November 2026 from RePEc.

The four code chunks below are used for loading libraries, specifying key assumptions, and importing and joining the data.

Code: setup

The code below loads the libraries, sets key assumptions and defines standard chart styles and labels for the rest of the post.

# load the packages we'll need
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(ggrepel)

#file paths
ref_path <- list(
  wgi            = file.path("Data", "wgidataset_with_sourcedata-2025.xlsx"),
  income_history = file.path("Data", "OGHIST_2026_10_08.xlsx"),  # World Bank historical income groups
  wdi            = file.path("Data", "261022 - wdi_indicators.csv"),  # WDI indicators and regions
  pacific        = file.path("Data", "261107 - pacific_island_small_states.csv")  # World Bank Pacific island small states
)

#years covered
ref_year <- list(
  start        = 1996,      # the first WGI year
  end          = 2023,      # the last year with near-complete WDI coverage for most series
  rents_window = 2019:2023  # the last five years, averaged for oil and gas rents, which swing with prices
)

#cut-offs that define samples and groups
ref_cutoff <- list(
  min_growth_years         = 20,  # countries with fewer years of growth data are dropped
  large_producer_rents_pct = 10,  # oil and gas rents above this share of GDP mark a large producer
  min_group_countries      = 5,   # region and income groups with fewer countries are left off the correlation chart
  outlier_sd               = 2    # countries further than this many standard deviations above the line are named on the growth chart
)

#WDI indicators: short name = World Bank code
ref_wdi_indicators <- c(
  econ_gdppc_ppp        = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD",   # GDP per capita, PPP, constant international $
  econ_gdppc_growth_pct = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD.ZG",   # GDP per capita growth, annual %
  pop_tot_nmb           = "SP.POP.TOTL",         # population
  res_oil_rents_pct     = "NY.GDP.PETR.RT.ZS",   # oil rents, % of GDP
  res_gas_rents_pct     = "NY.GDP.NGAS.RT.ZS"    # natural gas rents, % of GDP
)

#colours (from my site palette), set once for every chart
ref_col <- list(
  navy       = "#0C1446",  # titles and strip labels
  charcoal   = "#2B2E45",  # body text
  grey       = "#73768C",  # axis labels, captions, annotations
  grey_light = "#C7CBD8",  # background points and context
  grey_pale  = "#E2E8F0",  # gridlines and zero lines
  blue       = "#2740DA",  # the series the chart is about
  red        = "#922C40",  # decline
  orange     = "#DC9750",  # a second group shown beside the blue one
  green      = "#16AF8E"   # improvement
)
#red and green always mean decline and improvement; the four hues in order for charts with several groups
ref_col$direction <- c(Decline = ref_col$red, Improvement = ref_col$green)
ref_col$series    <- c(ref_col$blue, ref_col$red, ref_col$orange, ref_col$green)

#chart text: the source caption, how to read a WGI axis, and the large producer legend
# WGI scores run from about -2.5 to +2.5, centred on the average country.
# Arrows turn with the text on a vertical axis, so vertical axes get words instead.
ref_lab <- list(
  caption             = "Source: Worldwide Governance Indicators (2025); World Development Indicators.",
  axis_score          = "← weaker      0 = average country      stronger →",
  axis_score_vertical = "higher = stronger; 0 = average country",
  axis_change         = "← worsened      0 = no change      improved →",
  large_producers     = paste0("Oil and gas rents above ", ref_cutoff$large_producer_rents_pct, "% of GDP"),
  clear_of_error      = "* The change is larger than its 90% measurement band, which lies wholly on one side of zero.",
  income_start        = "Income groups are each country's earliest World Bank classification (for most, based on 1987 income), not its current one."
)

#series colours for charts with up to four groups
options(ggplot2.discrete.colour = ref_col$series,
        ggplot2.discrete.fill   = ref_col$series)

# Open Sans needs to be installed; ragg (set in the YAML) picks it up.
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11, base_family = "Open Sans") +
    theme(text                  = element_text(colour = ref_col$charcoal),
          axis.text             = element_text(colour = ref_col$grey),
          axis.title            = element_text(size = rel(0.9)),
          axis.title.x          = element_text(margin = margin(t = 8)),
          axis.title.y          = element_text(margin = margin(r = 8)),
          panel.grid.minor      = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x    = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.y    = element_line(colour = ref_col$grey_pale, linewidth = 0.4),
          strip.text            = element_text(colour = ref_col$navy, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
          legend.position       = "top",
          legend.justification  = "left",
          legend.title          = element_blank(),
          plot.title            = element_text(colour = ref_col$navy, face = "bold",
                                               size = rel(1.15)),
          plot.subtitle         = element_text(colour = ref_col$grey,
                                               margin = margin(b = 10)),
          plot.title.position   = "plot",
          plot.caption         = element_text(colour = ref_col$grey, face = "italic",
                                               size = rel(0.75), hjust = 0),
          plot.caption.position = "plot",
          plot.margin           = margin(10, 15, 10, 10))
)
update_geom_defaults("text", list(family = "Open Sans", colour = ref_col$charcoal))

Importing data

Code: import-wgi

The code below imports the WGI and recodes countries so they align with the World Bank data.

# Read the Rule of Law sheet. The sheet has one unnamed column; "unique_quiet"
# gives it a name without printing a message.
dta_wgi_rol <- read_excel(ref_path$wgi, sheet = "rl", .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
  clean_names()

# Keep the columns we need, with shorter names. Missing estimates may be
# stored as text (such as ".."), so the scores are converted to numbers.
dta_wgi_rol <- dta_wgi_rol |>
  mutate(year       = as.integer(year),
         wgi_rol    = as.numeric(governance_estimate_approx_2_5_to_2_5),
         wgi_rol_se = as.numeric(standard_error_estimate)) |>
  select(iso3c = economy_code, country = economy_name, year, wgi_rol, wgi_rol_se)

# Older WGI releases used a few codes that are not ISO codes. This lookup
# gives the ISO code for each one.
lkp_iso_fixes <- c(ROM = "ROU", ZAR = "COD", TMP = "TLS",
                   ADO = "AND", KSV = "XKX", WBG = "PSE")

# Swap in the ISO code where the lookup has one; otherwise keep the code as it is
dta_wgi_rol <- dta_wgi_rol |>
  mutate(iso3c = coalesce(unname(lkp_iso_fixes[iso3c]), iso3c))

Code: import-wdi

The code below imports the WDI data and the World Bank’s historical income classifications.

Each country is grouped by its earliest World Bank income classification to avoid the groups directly mirroring rule of law scores i.e. due to simultaneity between economic growth and the rule of law. This isn’t a perfect solution, but will have to suffice in the absence of an instrument.

# WDI indicators and World Bank regions, downloaded on 22 October 2026 with
# wbstats::wb_data(indicator = ref_wdi_indicators, start_date = 1996, end_date = 2023),
# and each country's region from wbstats::wb_countries(), with aggregates such as
# "World" dropped
dta_wdi <- read_csv(ref_path$wdi, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(iso3c, country, region, year, all_of(names(ref_wdi_indicators))) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year))

# Income group names: World Bank code = full name, and full name = short name for charts
lkp_income <- list(
  full  = c(L  = "Low income",          LM = "Lower middle income",
            UM = "Upper middle income", H  = "High income"),
  short = c("Low income"          = "Low",
            "Lower middle income" = "Lower middle",
            "Upper middle income" = "Upper middle",
            "High income"         = "High")
)

# The World Bank's historical income classifications. The fiscal years (FY89
# to FY27) are in row 5, so the four title rows above it are skipped. Every
# column is read as text, because the codes are letters. The first column
# holds the country code.
lkp_income_start <- read_excel(ref_path$income_history, sheet = "Country Analytical History",
                               skip = 4, col_types = "text", .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
  rename(iso3c = 1)

# Keep the country rows only. This drops the row of calendar years under the
# fiscal years, and the notes at the foot of the sheet.
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  filter(str_detect(iso3c, "^[A-Z]{3}$"))

# Reshape to one line per country and fiscal year
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("FY"), names_to = "fiscal_year", values_to = "income_code")

# Keep the years in which a country was classified. ".." means not classified
# that year. "LM*" is Yemen with a footnote, so the asterisk is removed first.
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  mutate(income_code = str_remove(income_code, "\\*")) |>
  filter(income_code %in% names(lkp_income$full))

# Turn the fiscal year into a number: FY89 to FY99 are 1989 to 1999, and FY00
# onwards are 2000 onwards
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  mutate(fiscal_year = as.integer(str_remove(fiscal_year, "FY")),
         fiscal_year = if_else(fiscal_year >= 80, 1900L + fiscal_year, 2000L + fiscal_year))

# Keep each country's earliest classification: slice_min() keeps the line with
# the smallest fiscal year for each country
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  slice_min(fiscal_year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = iso3c)

# The columns used in the rest of the post: the income group's full name, the
# fiscal year it comes from, and a simpler split of high income against
# everyone else, used in later charts
lkp_income_start <- lkp_income_start |>
  mutate(econ_income_start    = unname(lkp_income$full[income_code]),
         econ_income_start_fy = fiscal_year,
         econ_hic_start       = if_else(econ_income_start == "High income",
                                        "High income", "Low & middle income")) |>
  select(iso3c, econ_income_start, econ_income_start_fy, econ_hic_start)

# Number of countries in each starting income group
count(lkp_income_start, econ_income_start, econ_hic_start)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  econ_income_start   econ_hic_start          n
  <chr>               <chr>               <int>
1 High income         High income            54
2 Low income          Low & middle income    51
3 Lower middle income Low & middle income    78
4 Upper middle income Low & middle income    40

Code: join

The code below joins WGI and WDI datasets into a single panel dataset. Countries that failed to join are listed, as are countries scored in 1996 whose first income classification came later.

# Add the WGI scores to the WDI data, matching on country code and year. The
# WDI data already has the country names, so the WGI's are dropped.
dta_panel <- dta_wdi |>
  left_join(select(dta_wgi_rol, -country), by = join_by(iso3c, year), relationship = "one-to-one")

# Add each country's starting income group
dta_panel <- dta_panel |>
  left_join(lkp_income_start, by = join_by(iso3c), relationship = "many-to-one")

# WGI economies with no match in the WDI data. Most are territories, such as
# Jersey, or economies the World Bank doesn't cover, such as Taiwan.
chk_wgi_unmatched <- dta_wgi_rol |>
  distinct(iso3c, country) |>
  anti_join(distinct(dta_panel, iso3c), by = join_by(iso3c))

chk_wgi_unmatched
# A tibble: 9 × 2
  iso3c country                      
  <chr> <chr>                        
1 GUF   French Guiana                
2 MTQ   Martinique                   
3 TWN   Taiwan, China                
4 AIA   Anguilla                     
5 ANT   Netherlands Antilles (former)
6 REU   Réunion                      
7 COK   Cook Islands                 
8 NIU   Niue                         
9 JEY   Jersey, Channel Islands      
# Countries scored in 1996 whose first income classification came after 1996
chk_income_late <- dta_panel |>
  filter(year == ref_year$start, !is.na(wgi_rol)) |>
  filter(is.na(econ_income_start) | econ_income_start_fy > ref_year$start) |>
  select(iso3c, country, econ_income_start, econ_income_start_fy)

chk_income_late
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  iso3c country econ_income_start   econ_income_start_fy

Global rule of law trends

To get a sense how the rule of law has changed, the code block below calculates the average rule of law score since 1996 across countries. Both unweighted and population-weighted scores are calculated, with the latter indicating how the rule of law has changed for the average person.

Note: Revisions to the WGI’s methodology in 2025 improve the ability for scores to be compared over time (see the World Bank’s methodology note, cited in the Data section above).

Code: population-weighted-trends

The code below calculates the global unweighted and weighted rule of law score. Only countries with WGI scores in the first year are included so the number of countries remain fixed.

# The countries with a score in 1996. Only these countries are kept, so the
# same countries are averaged in every year.
ref_countries_1996 <- dta_panel |>
  filter(year == ref_year$start, !is.na(wgi_rol)) |>
  pull(iso3c)

# Keep those countries, in every year where they have a score, a standard
# error, a population and a starting income group
dta_panel_1996 <- dta_panel |>
  filter(iso3c %in% ref_countries_1996,
         !is.na(wgi_rol),
         !is.na(wgi_rol_se),
         !is.na(pop_tot_nmb),
         !is.na(econ_income_start))

# Order the income groups from poorest to richest (by the median GDP per
# capita of each group), so charts list them in that order
dta_panel_1996 <- dta_panel_1996 |>
  mutate(econ_income_start = fct_reorder(econ_income_start, econ_gdppc_ppp,
                                         .fun = median, .na_rm = TRUE))

# The world average in each year, weighted by population and unweighted.
# Each standard error combines the WGI's country standard errors using the
# same weights as the average. This assumes the measurement errors of
# different countries are independent of one another.
sum_rol_world_avg <- dta_panel_1996 |>
  summarise(
    wgi_rol_popw    = weighted.mean(wgi_rol, w = pop_tot_nmb),
    wgi_rol_unw     = mean(wgi_rol),
    wgi_rol_popw_se = sqrt(sum((pop_tot_nmb / sum(pop_tot_nmb))^2 * wgi_rol_se^2)),
    wgi_rol_unw_se  = sqrt(sum(wgi_rol_se^2)) / n(),
    nmb_countries   = n(),
    .by = year) |>
  arrange(year)

# Change in the weighted average since 1996
sum_rol_world_avg <- sum_rol_world_avg |>
  mutate(wgi_rol_popw_change = wgi_rol_popw - wgi_rol_popw[year == ref_year$start])

# The change from 1996 to 2023, quoted in the text below
sum_rol_world_change <- sum_rol_world_avg$wgi_rol_popw_change[sum_rol_world_avg$year == ref_year$end]

The rule of law has declined globally

The chart below presents weighted and unweighted rule of law scores since 1996. Unweighted scores can be thought of as how the rule of law has changed for the average country, while the weighted scores are intended to show how it has changed for the average person. In both cases the rule of law appears to have declined globally, although the declines in unweighted scores only just clear the measurement error bands.

Note: Shaded bands are based on the standard errors provided by the WGI and can be thought of as margins of error. In their note on analytical issues with the WGI, Kaufmann, Kraay and Mastruzzi suggest that overlapping intervals can be thought of as a conservative test for whether two scores are the same.3 And while the generalized declines might be cause for alarm, the population-weighted fall of 0.22 is smaller than the 0.31 difference in scores between Denmark and New Zealand in 2023. This doesn’t mean that the changes aren’t significant from a governance standpoint, but just that the scale of these declines doesn’t necessarily point to the world becoming lawless.

# How much each country added to, or took away from, the change in the
# weighted world average. The weighted average in a year is the sum, across
# countries, of population share x score. So a country's contribution to the
# change is its share x score in 2023 less its share x score in 1996, and the
# contributions add up to the change in the world line exactly.

# Step 1: each country's share of the total population in 1996 and in 2023
dta_country_contrib <- dta_panel_1996 |>
  filter(year %in% c(ref_year$start, ref_year$end)) |>
  mutate(pop_share = pop_tot_nmb / sum(pop_tot_nmb), .by = year) |>
  mutate(period = if_else(year == ref_year$start, "start", "end")) |>
  select(iso3c, country, period, pop_share, wgi_rol, wgi_rol_se)

# Step 2: put the two years side by side, one line per country, with the
# columns pop_share_start, pop_share_end, wgi_rol_start, wgi_rol_end,
# wgi_rol_se_start and wgi_rol_se_end
dta_country_contrib <- dta_country_contrib |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = c(pop_share, wgi_rol, wgi_rol_se))

# Step 3: each country's contribution, and its change in score
dta_country_contrib <- dta_country_contrib |>
  mutate(contrib        = pop_share_end * wgi_rol_end - pop_share_start * wgi_rol_start,
         wgi_rol_change = wgi_rol_end - wgi_rol_start)

# The five most populous countries in 2023, quoted in the text below and
# charted in the next chunk
dta_most_populous <- dta_country_contrib |>
  slice_max(pop_share_end, n = 5)

# Is each change clear of measurement error? The standard error of the change
# combines the 1996 and 2023 errors, treating them as independent, as for the
# region and income groups below. A change is clear when its whole 90% band
# (1.645 standard errors either side) lies on one side of zero.
dta_most_populous <- dta_most_populous |>
  mutate(wgi_rol_change_se = sqrt(wgi_rol_se_start^2 + wgi_rol_se_end^2),
         clear_of_error    = abs(wgi_rol_change) > 1.645 * wgi_rol_change_se)

dta_most_populous <- dta_most_populous |>
  mutate(direction     = if_else(wgi_rol_change < 0, "Decline", "Improvement"),
         # the axis label, for example "India (18% of population)", with an
         # asterisk after the name when the change is clear of measurement error
         country_label = sprintf("%s%s (%.0f%% of population)", country,
                                 if_else(clear_of_error, "*", ""), pop_share_end * 100),
         # order the labels by population, so the largest is at the top of the chart
         country_label = fct_reorder(country_label, pop_share_end))

India was a key driver of global declines in the rule of law

Population-weighted average rule of law scores mean more populous countries with larger score changes drive the global average. The code below explores this by looking at the source of declines, with a focus on the five most populated countries (accounting for 46% of world population).

The answer is mixed, with India, the United States and Pakistan experiencing declines, Indonesia an improvement and China showing next to no net change. Although India experienced smaller declines relative to the United States and Pakistan, its larger population made it a key driver of declines in the global weighted average rule of law score.

When each country’s score is viewed individually, the trends aren’t as clear cut. For instance, although India’s score has declined over the period, the change is within the bounds for measurement error, making it possible that score differences come down to measurement error rather than tangible changes in institutional quality (which is also true for China). On the other hand, the trends exhibited by the United States and Indonesia are large enough to point to real changes over the period: a decline for the former and improvement for the latter.

Countries with stronger rule of law are richer

You don’t need to be an economist to guess that the rule of law is probably stronger in richer countries5, but scatter plots demonstrating this appear in almost every governance report talking about the rule of law. The plot below demonstrates this by comparing each country’s rule of law score in 2023 with its GDP per capita. Purchasing power parity (PPP) terms are used to adjust for differences in purchasing power, such that one PPP dollar has the same real value across countries.

The line on the plot shows the typical relationship between the rule of law and average income. Countries to the left of the line are poorer than might be expected given their rule of law scores, while those to the right of the line are wealthier. Although why countries sit on either side is a rabbit hole worth exploring, a large share of the outliers can be explained by geography and the structure of a country’s economy, in particular:

  • Countries that are wealthier than might be expected given their rule of law score: include economies that rely heavily on oil and gas rents, which is theorised to reduce the incentive for government to create inclusive institutions for the benefit of the wider public.6
  • Countries that are poorer than might be expected given their rule of law score: include a large share of Pacific island economies and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. While the reasons are beyond the scope of this post, Pacific island economies are unusually small and remote, depressing economic activity and trade, while many of the countries in Sub-Saharan Africa face wider institutional and geographic challenges, such as poor governance and having a smaller share of their population near navigable rivers.7

As always, my point here isn’t to imply the two things are causally connected as the claim requires more evidence than a pairwise correlation. But, the idea that more secure, predictable and legible property rights might make trade and commerce easier isn’t new, which means there’s plenty of evidence exploring the idea.8 It’s also a compelling idea to anybody who has spent their career being inundated with governance reports presenting the correlation.

But, there’s also an arguable conceptual endogeneity9 between GDP per capita and the rule of law. The rule of law plays a central role in deciding what can be owned, priced and traded, while also being shaped by the same political and economic forces it is meant to govern.10 So by strengthening the rule of law, what can be owned, priced and traded changes too,11 thereby expanding what can be counted in GDP statistics. That doesn’t make the connection meaningless as GDP is connected with other things we care about like life expectancy and wellbeing. But it’s good to keep in mind as it’s likely that some part of the correlation reflects their overlapping and mutually reinforcing scope, rather than simply being a clean relationship between two independent variables.

Note: Oil and gas rents are the value of oil and gas production less what it costs to extract, as a share of GDP, from the World Development Indicators.

       y = paste0("Rule of Law estimate (WGI units)\n", ref_lab$axis_score_vertical),
       caption = paste(ref_lab$caption, "World Bank country classifications."))

plt_rol_income

But economic growth without the rule of law exists

Almost every discussion of the links between institutions and economic growth eventually turns to China. China, so the story goes, has grown quickly without investing in pesky institutions like the rule of law.12 This section tests that story in two steps: first by comparing growth with where countries started on the rule of law in 1996, and then by comparing growth with how their rule of law changed over the period.

The plot below shows the distribution of average GDP per capita growth from 1997 to 2023, with countries grouped into four groups based on their rule of law score in 1996. It’s as good a time as any to repeat the warning about drawing sweeping conclusions from observational analysis like this, but the data suggests two things about economic growth and the rule of law:

  1. Strong growth is possible where the rule of law is weak: many of the countries that started with weak scores grew faster than those that started with strong ones; and
  2. A strong rule of law doesn’t guarantee high growth: the countries with the strongest rule of law scores in 1996 had the lowest median growth of the four groups.13

Note: Most of the countries in the strongest quarter were already high income at the start of the period, and richer countries tend to grow more slowly, partly because they have less room to catch up.

Figure: Average growth 1997–2023 by Rule of Law in 1996

Code: plot-growth-vs-start

The code below calculates the average annual economic growth and presents this as a histogram with countries grouped according to their rule of law score in 1996.

# One line per country: its score in 1996 and 2023, and its average growth.
# Growth in 1996 itself happened before the starting score, so it is left out.
# first() returns the single value for that year, or NA if the country has none.
# Some countries miss a few years of growth, hence na.rm = TRUE.
dta_country_growth <- dta_panel |>
  summarise(
    wgi_rol_start       = first(wgi_rol[year == ref_year$start]),
    wgi_rol_end         = first(wgi_rol[year == ref_year$end]),
    wgi_rol_se_start    = first(wgi_rol_se[year == ref_year$start]),
    wgi_rol_se_end      = first(wgi_rol_se[year == ref_year$end]),
    econ_growth_avg_pct = mean(econ_gdppc_growth_pct[year > ref_year$start], na.rm = TRUE),
    nmb_growth_years    = sum(!is.na(econ_gdppc_growth_pct[year > ref_year$start])),
    .by = c(iso3c, country, region))

# Keep countries with a 1996 score and at least 20 years of growth data, then
# add the change in score and the starting income group
dta_country_growth <- dta_country_growth |>
  filter(!is.na(wgi_rol_start),
         nmb_growth_years >= ref_cutoff$min_growth_years) |>
  mutate(wgi_rol_change = wgi_rol_end - wgi_rol_start) |>
  left_join(lkp_income_start, by = join_by(iso3c), relationship = "one-to-one")

# Panel titles, weakest starting score first
lkp_quarter_titles <- c("Weakest quarter of 1996 Rule of Law scores", "Second-weakest quarter",
                 "Second-strongest quarter", "Strongest quarter of 1996 Rule of Law scores")

# ntile() splits the countries into four equal-sized groups by their 1996 score,
# 1 being the weakest. rev() reverses the panel order only, so the strongest
# quarter is drawn at the top.
dta_country_growth <- dta_country_growth |>
  mutate(start_quarter       = ntile(wgi_rol_start, 4),
         start_quarter_label = factor(lkp_quarter_titles[start_quarter], levels = rev(lkp_quarter_titles)))

# Median, spread and counts for each quarter, used in the chart and the note
# above it (how many in each quarter started as high income)
sum_growth_quarter <- dta_country_growth |>
  summarise(nmb_countries   = n(),
            nmb_high_income = sum(econ_hic_start == "High income"),
            growth_median   = median(econ_growth_avg_pct),
            growth_sd       = sd(econ_growth_avg_pct),
            growth_p10      = quantile(econ_growth_avg_pct, 0.1),
            growth_p90      = quantile(econ_growth_avg_pct, 0.9),
            .by = c(start_quarter, start_quarter_label)) |>
  arrange(start_quarter)

Countries where the rule of law improved were more likely to grow faster

The histogram above looked at growth against a country’s level of rule of law in 1996. The plot below looks at growth against the change in its rule of law score between 1996 and 2023.

In essence, it asks whether countries whose rule of law improved more also grew faster. The answer is a qualified yes, and the relationship is positive in every region with enough countries to measure it.

This isn’t to say that improvements in the rule of law cause economic growth14, only that the two have moved together over the last three decades. Causality could run the other way, with faster-growing countries able to spend more on the courts, police and other systems that support the rule of law, or it could run both ways. Other drivers of growth may also be missing from the analysis, such as the quality of regulation and political accountability, which are closely tied to the rule of law. Even so, the pattern helps explain why economists are so excited to talk about how and why the two might be linked.

The plot also highlights countries that grew faster than might be expected given changes in their score. China, the example that everyone raises, is there but isn’t alone: Equatorial Guinea, Guyana, Myanmar, Armenia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina all sit well above the line with no clear change in their rule of law score. Several have likely explanations, such as oil discoveries, economic recovery after war and the breakdown of the Soviet Union. China’s small change over the period also hides a fall in its score in the mid-2000s which was followed by a long recovery. None of this is to deny that China holds lessons about institutions and growth (it does), only that it’s not the only outlier that’s worth explaining.

Note: North America showed the opposite relationship but is left off the regional chart, as it has only three countries (Bermuda, Canada and the United States).

Figures: Change in Rule of Law and average growth, 1996–2023, for all countries and by region

Code: plot-growth-vs-change

The code below produces two plots: a scatter plot comparing economic growth with changes in the rule of law, with the unusually fast growers whose score didn’t clearly change named, and a bar plot that reports the correlation between the two variables within each region.

# The countries in the histograms that have a score in 2023 as well as 1996
dta_growth_change <- dta_country_growth |>
  filter(!is.na(wgi_rol_change))

# How far each country's growth sits above or below the straight line drawn
# through all countries, in percentage points
dta_growth_change <- dta_growth_change |>
  mutate(growth_vs_line = residuals(lm(econ_growth_avg_pct ~ wgi_rol_change)))

# The countries named on the chart: growth more than two standard deviations
# of these distances above the line, and a change in score inside its 90%
# measurement band, worked out as for the five most populous countries
dta_growth_change <- dta_growth_change |>
  mutate(wgi_rol_change_se  = sqrt(wgi_rol_se_start^2 + wgi_rol_se_end^2),
         change_within_band = abs(wgi_rol_change) <= 1.645 * wgi_rol_change_se,
         fast_no_change     = growth_vs_line > ref_cutoff$outlier_sd * sd(growth_vs_line) &
                              change_within_band)

plt_growth_change <- dta_growth_change |>
  ggplot(aes(x = wgi_rol_change, y = econ_growth_avg_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ref_col$grey_pale) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ref_col$grey_pale) +
  geom_point(colour = ref_col$blue, alpha = 0.6) +
  # one straight-line fit through all countries, with no controls
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = ref_col$grey, linewidth = 0.8) +
  # name the fast growers whose score didn't clearly change, China among them.
  # Each label is joined to its point by a short line (min.segment.length = 0 always draws it).
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(dta_growth_change, fast_no_change),
                  aes(label = country), size = 3, colour = ref_col$charcoal,
                  family = "Open Sans", seed = 1, min.segment.length = 0) +
  labs(title    = "Countries whose Rule of Law improved grew faster than those where it declined",
       subtitle = "Each country's average growth against its change in score; straight-line fit, no controls",
       x = paste0("Change in Rule of Law, 1996–2023 (WGI units)\n", ref_lab$axis_change),
       y = "Average GDP per capita growth, 1997–2023 (% a year)",
       caption = paste(sprintf("Named: growth more than %d standard deviations above the line, and a change in score inside its 90%% measurement band.",
                               ref_cutoff$outlier_sd),
                       ref_lab$caption, sep = "\n"))

# Correlation between the change in score and average growth within each region
sum_cor_region <- dta_growth_change |>
  summarise(nmb_countries = n(),
            cor_change    = cor(wgi_rol_change, econ_growth_avg_pct),
            .by = region)

# Regions with fewer countries than the cut-off are left off the chart. On the
# data used here (checked 10 November 2026) this is North America (3 countries:
# Bermuda, Canada and the United States).
sum_cor_small_regions <- sum_cor_region |>
  filter(nmb_countries < ref_cutoff$min_group_countries)

# Keep the regions large enough to chart
sum_cor_region <- sum_cor_region |>
  filter(nmb_countries >= ref_cutoff$min_group_countries)

# Is each correlation statistically significant at the 10% level, matching the
# 90% bands used elsewhere in the post? This is the standard test that the
# correlation is zero, written out: the t statistic is
# r x sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r^2)), with n - 2 degrees of freedom. It gives the
# same p-value as cor.test().
sum_cor_region <- sum_cor_region |>
  mutate(cor_t       = cor_change * sqrt((nmb_countries - 2) / (1 - cor_change^2)),
         cor_p_value = 2 * pt(-abs(cor_t), df = nmb_countries - 2),
         cor_signif  = cor_p_value < 0.10)

# The labels: an asterisk after the region when the correlation is significant,
# and the number of countries in brackets
sum_cor_region <- sum_cor_region |>
  mutate(region_label = sprintf("%s%s (%d)", region, if_else(cor_signif, "*", ""), nmb_countries),
         # largest correlation at the top
         region_label = fct_reorder(region_label, cor_change))

plt_cor_region <- sum_cor_region |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cor_change, y = region_label)) +
  geom_col(fill = ref_col$blue, width = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ref_col$grey) +
  # the value sits just beyond the end of each bar
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", cor_change)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = ref_col$grey_pale, linewidth = 0.4)) +
  labs(title    = sprintf("Improvement went with faster growth in %d of %d regions",
                          sum(sum_cor_region$cor_change > 0),
                          nrow(sum_cor_region)),
       subtitle = sprintf("Correlation within each region, countries in brackets; regions under %d countries left out",
                          ref_cutoff$min_group_countries),
       x = "Correlation between change in Rule of Law and average growth, 1996–2023",
       y = NULL, caption = paste("* Statistically significant at the 10% level: the correlation's 90% interval excludes zero.",
                                 ref_lab$caption, sep = "\n"))

Summing up

The point of this post, besides satisfying my curiosity about the data, was to lay out a set of common themes that emerge in the literature:

  • Globally, the rule of law has deteriorated since the mid 90s;
  • The rule of law and economic growth appear to be linked;
  • The rule of law’s relationship with economic growth is positive across regions; and
  • The rule of law isn’t a necessary or sufficient condition for economic growth.

If you’re familiar with the field, none of this will be particularly surprising, but each of these themes provides useful context for future posts where I attempt to tease out some of these relationships and trends in greater detail. But, I also wanted to make a contribution to the grey literature on the topic as from my observations there are few explorations of the topic that dig into the technical details outside published papers on the topic.
